question: European leaders have increasingly warned China against supplying arms and dual-use goods to Russia. According to Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy (VP/HR) Josep Borrell, this would cross a ‘red line’.

Citing intelligence sources, recent media reports claim that a Chinese factory is producing combat drones for Russia1, and that Russia has launched an arms programme in China to develop and produce long-range combat drones for use in the war against Ukraine2. VP/HR Borrell stresses that China is the main supplier of the dual-use goods and sensitive technologies that underpin Russia’s military-industrial base. 1.
Are these reports true and, if so, what concrete consequences does the new VP/HR believe these reports will have on the EU’s relationship with China?
What measures will the new VP/HR take to prevent dual-use technologies or products from mainland China and Hong Kong entering Russia in the future?
How will the new VP/HR coordinate these measures with partner countries, for example the G7 countries, South Korea and Australia?

South China Morning Post (15 November 2024), EU has ‘conclusive’ proof of armed drones for Russia being made in China, https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomacy/article/3286819/eu-has-conclusive-proofarmed-drones-russia-being-made-china-sources. Reuters (25 September 2024), Exclusive: Russia has secret war drones project in China, intel sources say, https://www.reuters.com/world/russia-has-secret-war-drones-project-china-intel-sources-say-2024-09-25/.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.2.2025) China is a key enabler of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. China’s support comes with a cost. It negatively affects EU-China relations. China is the largest provider of dual-use goods and sensitive items that sustain Russia’s military industrial base and that are found on the battlefield in Ukraine.
These goods are used in multiple types of military equipment. Without China's support, Russia would not be able to continue its military aggression with the same force.

Since the start of the EU’s sanctions against Russia, the EU has placed 33 entities based in mainland China or Hong Kong on a list of specific export restrictions1 because these entities have been found to export to Russia sanctioned dual-use and advanced tech components, including of EU origin, which are used by the Russian army to wage war against Ukraine.

For the first time since the start of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, with the 15th package of sanctions, the EU also imposed fully-fledged sanctions (travel ban, asset freeze, prohibition to make funds and economic resources available) on six Chinese companies and one Chinese individual supplying drone components and microelectronic components in support of Russia’s war effort.

The EU will continue to take appropriate measures to avoid sanctions circumvention and stem the supply of components, including of EU origin, used by the Russian army on the battlefield, including by coordinating with like-minded partners.
1 Annex IV to Council Regulation (EU) No 833/2014.
